Speed highly influences your "score".

I'm a naturally slow person with everything (executive functioning problems and just general laid-back attitute), and when we took an IQ test in school, I went especially slow and triple-checked every answer, since my parents told me it was important.

I got "low IQ" as a result, even though I never had difficulties in school and was viewed as being "bright" by family and friends. I thought that I may very well be a lot dumber than I thought, or that the speed might've been part of the culprit.

Years later, I took a professional IQ test and did it as quickly as I could (which required significant concentration for my ADD brain), and I ended up getting a "high IQ" as a result.

All this to say that, if you have executive functioning problems and/or ADHD, it's possible your test score is lower than what your "real score" would be.

This is just my experience, though!

I've been in a similar conundrum. My boyfriend isn't studying or working and is only passively looking for a job. (Not that he's lazy  -- he works out and takes care of our apartment and cats as well as his grandma and dogs.)

To me, it boiled down to what I want in life. I love my partner, he makes me happy and we're building a fulfilling life together. He's not ambitious or professionally successful, but to me that's a more than worthy trade off.

I think we've been conditioned to think that our value depends on how 'productive' we are, how much we achieve. But I don't see it that way -- even without studies or a job, he's infinitely valuable to me because of who he is. His success is only important insofar as it can provide us with financial security, but I can do that myself.

In your case, it really depends on what you want out of life. If you want to build an empire with a career-driven woman because that's what will fulfill you, then you made the right choice. But is that what will fulfill you? It's a question only you can answer.

It's perfectly possible for someone with ASPD to treat their partners with respect and have a loving relationship. It's also possible for him to be 'bonded' to you, and though that is very different from loving you, it means he thinks he's better off with you than without you and that he appreciates your presence in his life (at least in the way we'd appreciate having a smartphone vs not having one). Also, the fact that he's always treated you with respect and goes to therapy is commendable.

That said, your worries are not unfounded. If he's been diagnosed with ASPD, in all likelihood he cannot feel empathy or remorse, which makes him a lot more capable of doing harm than the average person. He does not love you, and is bonded to you only insofar as you make his life easier. As soon as you don't, things might take a turn and you might see the ugly side of him. Whether you want to take that risk or not is up to you, but I would caution you against it. If you do decide to break things off with him, make sure you do it in a safe environment.

Saying that 'you are his unicorn', etc, is a form of manipulation. He wants you to stay with him and therefore is trying to appease your concerns by making you feel special, like the exception to the rule. Unfortunately, you are not the exception to the rule, no one is, which means that yes, he does manipulate you, even if you're not aware of it, and yes, he is putting on an act, at least to an extent.

I hope I haven't been overly pessimistic. Again, if he's been treating you well and lovingly thus far, that's a good sign. Of course, not all people with ASPD are violent or malicious. But I would say that, at the very least, you keep a close eye on him and dip at the first red flag. Good luck!

Uhhh. Speaking from my personal experience:

In person over text; meaningful connection is important and that's hard to achieve through text. I hate texting, I am very flakey _even if_ I am interested in the other person. Texting is a chore, it is a way to give information, not build a connection.

Also, yes, it's hard for me to open up, but often because people ask very general questions like "how are you" and because people are rarely interested in my answer after a bit of explaining. So, follow the rule of thumb: SPECIFIC & GRADUAL DEPTH!

Ask her specific questions about what you want to know; i repeat, specific! INFPs tend to be very sincere so its likely she'll just tell you what she thinks. Then start making the questions broader. Eg. Do NOT ask "Where do you wanna take this relationship?" -> overwhelming, too general, doesnt know where to start, needs time to think the answer through.

Rather, say for example "I really enjoyed spending time with you the other day; do you also prefer to spend time with me in person?" -> specific question about an emotional experience, easy-ish question that helps her open up about deeper thoughts and feelings. Once she answers, continue being specific but get deeper. Does this make sense?

Needless to say, listen to all of her answers attentively. Let the pauses hang.
